title: Chapter 94 — A Squeeze of the Hand
paragraphs: That whale of Stubb's, so dearly purchased, was duly brought to the Pequod's side, where all those cutting and hoisting operations previously described were regularly gone through, even to the bailing of the Heidelburgh Tun, or Case.

While some were occupied with this latter duty, others were employed in dragging away the larger tubs as soon as they were filled with sperm. And when the proper time arrived, this same sperm was carefully processed before going to the try-works, of which more later.

It had cooled and crystallized to such a degree that when, with several others, I sat down before a large bath of it, I found it strangely congealed into lumps, here and there rolling about in the liquid part. It was our business to squeeze these lumps back into fluid. A sweet and oily duty! No wonder that in old times this sperm was such a favorite cosmetic. Such a cleanser! Such a sweetener! Such a softener! Such a delicious emollient! After having my hands in it for only a few minutes, my fingers felt like eels and began, as it were, to coil and spiral.

As I sat there at my ease, cross-legged on the deck — after the bitter exertion at the windlass, under a blue tranquil sky, the ship under lazy sail and gliding so serenely along — as I bathed my hands among those soft, gentle globules of infiltrated tissue, woven almost within the hour, as they richly broke to my fingers and discharged all their richness, like fully ripe grapes their wine, as I breathed in that uncontaminated aroma, literally and truly like the smell of spring violets — I declare to you that for the time I lived as in a musky meadow. I forgot all about our horrible oath. In that inexpressible sperm, I washed my hands and my heart of it. I almost began to credit the old superstition that sperm is of rare virtue in calming the heat of anger. While bathing in that bath, I felt divinely free from all ill-will, or irritation, or malice of any sort whatsoever.

Squeeze! Squeeze! Squeeze! All the morning long I squeezed that sperm till I myself almost melted into it. I squeezed that sperm till a strange sort of madness came over me, and I found myself unwittingly squeezing my co-workers' hands in it, mistaking their hands for the gentle globules. Such an overflowing, affectionate, friendly, loving feeling did this work beget that at last I was continually squeezing their hands and looking up into their eyes sentimentally — as much as to say: Oh, my dear fellow beings, why should we any longer harbor any social bitterness, or know the slightest ill-humor or envy! Come, let us squeeze hands all round. Nay, let us all squeeze ourselves into each other. Let us squeeze ourselves universally into the very milk and sperm of kindness.

Would that I could keep squeezing that sperm forever! For now, since by many prolonged, repeated experiences I have perceived that in all cases man must eventually lower, or at least shift, his idea of attainable happiness — not placing it anywhere in the intellect or the imagination but in the wife, the heart, the bed, the table, the saddle, the fireside, the country — now that I have perceived all this, I am ready to squeeze case eternally. In visions of the night, I saw long rows of angels in paradise, each with his hands in a jar of spermaceti.
Now, while speaking of sperm, it is fitting to mention other things related to it in the business of preparing the sperm whale for the try-works.

First comes white-horse, so called, which is obtained from the tapering part of the fish and also from the thicker portions of his flukes. It is tough with congealed tendons — a wad of muscle — but still contains some oil. After being severed from the whale, the white-horse is first cut into portable blocks before going to the mincer. They look much like blocks of marble.

Plum-pudding is the term bestowed upon certain fragmentary parts of the whale's flesh, here and there adhering to the blanket of blubber and often sharing considerably in its oiliness. It is a most refreshing, sociable, beautiful object to behold. As its name implies, it is of an exceedingly rich, mottled tint, with a streaked snowy and golden background dotted with spots of the deepest crimson and purple. It is plums of rubies in pictures of citron. Despite all reason, it is hard to keep yourself from eating it. I confess that once I stole behind the foremast to try it. It tasted something as I should imagine a royal cutlet from the thigh of Louis le Gros might have tasted, supposing him to have been killed the first day after the venison season, and that particular season contemporary with an unusually fine vintage of Champagne.

There is another substance, a very singular one, which turns up in the course of this business, but which I find very difficult to adequately describe. It is called slobgollion — a name original with the whalemen, and so is the nature of the substance. It is an indescribably oozy, stringy affair, most frequently found in the tubs of sperm after a prolonged squeezing and subsequent decanting. I hold it to be the wondrously thin, ruptured membranes of the case, fused together.

Gurry, so called, is a term properly belonging to right whalemen but sometimes used by the sperm fishermen as well. It designates the dark, glutinous substance which is scraped off the back of the Greenland or right whale, and much of which covers the decks of those inferior souls who hunt that ignoble Leviathan.

Nippers. Strictly, this word is not native to the whale's vocabulary. But as applied by whalemen, it becomes so. A whaleman's nipper is a short, firm strip of tough material cut from the tapering part of Leviathan's tail. It averages an inch in thickness and is otherwise about the size of the iron part of a hoe. Moved edgewise along the oily deck, it works like a leather squeegee, and by nameless magic, attracts along with it all impurities.

But to learn all about these obscure matters, your best course is to go straight down into the blubber-room and have a long talk with its inmates. This place has previously been mentioned as the receptacle for the blanket-pieces when stripped and hoisted from the whale. When the time comes to cut up its contents, this room becomes a scene of terror to all newcomers, especially at night. On one side, lit by a dull lantern, a space has been cleared for the workmen. They generally go in pairs — a pike-and-gaff man and a spademan. The whaling-pike is similar to a warship's boarding-weapon of the same name. The gaff is something like a boat-hook. With his gaff, the gaffman hooks onto a sheet of blubber and tries to hold it from slipping as the ship pitches and lurches about. Meanwhile, the spademan stands on the sheet itself, chopping it perpendicularly into portable horse-pieces. This spade is as sharp as a whetstone can make it. The spademan's feet are shoeless. The thing he stands on will sometimes irresistibly slide away from him like a sled. If he cuts off one of his own toes, or one of his assistant's, would you be very much surprised? Toes are scarce among veteran blubber-room men.
